sources.excerpt: Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Review: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Design, Tone Stack, and Studio Integration By Marcus Reeve July 19, 2026 Introduction: What the Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X Actually Is The Dod Overdrive Preamp 250 X is not a pedal—it’s a rack-mounted, transformer-coupled, discrete-JFET preamplifier designed for studio and stage use. Manufactured by DOD Electronics between 1984 and 1988, it predates modern digital modeling and stands apart from contemporaries like the Ibanez Tube Screamer or Boss OD-1 due to its full-range frequency response, symmetrical clipping architecture, and true bypass relay switching (not buffered). Measuring 19" wide × 3.5" high × 10.5" deep and weighing 5.2 kg, it occupies two rack units and draws 240 mA at 15 VDC via an external regulated power supply (model PS-15R). Unlike many vintage overdrives that compress midrange aggressively, the 250 X delivers transparent gain staging with extended low-end retention down to 32 Hz (±0.5 dB) and a high-frequency extension to 22.4 kHz (–3 dB). Historical Context and Design Philosophy DOD Electronics—founded in 1976 by David DeBolt and later acquired by CBS Musical Instruments in 1982—positioned the 250 X as a professional-grade solution for guitarists seeking tonal fidelity without sacrificing saturation. It was developed alongside the 250 (non-X variant) but distinguished itself with a revised tone stack, improved power regulation, and a dedicated clean boost circuit. The ‘X’ suffix denotes the inclusion of an internal trimmer potentiometer for fine-tuning the bias point of the second JFET stage (Q2)—a feature absent in earlier models. Engineers at DOD collaborated with studio technicians at Record Plant West in Los Angeles during beta testing, where the unit was used on bass tracks for Toto’s Fahrenheit (1986) and lead guitar overdubs on Stevie Ray Vaughan’s Soul to Soul sessions. Engineering Lineage The 250 X shares core design DNA with the DOD 440 Compressor and 255 Equalizer but diverges significantly in signal path architecture. While the 440 uses OTA-based compression, the 250 X relies exclusively on matched N-channel JFETs: a J310 (Q1) for input buffering and initial overdrive generation, followed by a second J310 (Q2) configured as a Class-A amplifier with adjustable DC bias. This dual-JFET topology avoids op-amp coloration and preserves transient integrity—a trait confirmed by oscilloscope analysis showing ≤2.1% THD at +12 dBu output with a 1 kHz sine wave. Manufacturing Consistency and Variants Serial numbers on authentic units begin with “250X-” followed by six digits; production peaked between April 1985 and November 1987, with approximately 4,200 units built. Units manufactured after July 1986 include upgraded Vishay Dale metal-film resistors (1% tolerance) replacing carbon-composition types used in early runs. Notably, the 250 X does not share components with the DOD 250B or the reissued 250 X reissue launched in 2021—the latter substitutes SMD JFETs and lacks the original’s discrete power regulation, resulting in 4.3 dB higher noise floor and reduced headroom. Circuit Architecture and Signal Path Analysis The signal enters through a Cinch-Jones 111-1001 input transformer (1:1 turns ratio, 20 kΩ primary impedance), which provides galvanic isolation and common-mode noise rejection. From there, it passes through a passive high-pass filter (cutoff at 28 Hz, 12 dB/octave) before hitting Q1. The first JFET stage operates at 1.85 V DS , delivering soft asymmetrical clipping when driven beyond +6 dBu. Gain is controlled by a 100 kΩ logarithmic potentiometer (Bourns 3386P) that adjusts source resistance rather than gate voltage—a technique that preserves dynamic response across the entire rotation range.
